truncation of $N/D$ and not to the Pad\'e slack.

\subsection{The derivative bracket}

\begin{lemma}[Two certified logarithms]\label{lem:logs}
\[
\log\frac{639}{79} \le 2.0904568254,
\qquad
2.0904563381 \le \log\frac{88997213}{11002787}.
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Both ratios are close to $8$: write $\frac{639}{79} = 8\cdot\frac{639}{632}$ and
$\frac{88997213}{11002787} = 8\cdot\frac{88997213}{88022296}$, and use
$\log 8 = 3\log 2$ with a nine-digit two-sided bound
$0.6931471803 < \log 2 < 0.6931471808$. The residual factors are within about
$1.11\times10^{-2}$ of $1$, so Lemma~\ref{lem:pade} applies with ample accuracy:
$\log\frac{639}{632} \le \frac12\left(\frac{639}{632} - \frac{632}{639}\right)
= \frac{8897}{807696}$ and
$\log\frac{88997213}{88022296} \ge \frac{2\cdot 974917}{177019509}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Derivative bracket at the anchor scale]\label{thm:deriv}
For all $x \in \left[\frac{79}{718},\; 0.11002787\right]$,
\[
2.0904563381 \;\le\; \log(1-x) - \log x \;\le\; 2.0904568254 ,
\]
a bracket of width $4.873\times 10^{-7}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
$x \mapsto \log(1-x) - \log x$ is strictly decreasing, so the maximum is at the
left endpoint, where the value is $\log\frac{639/718}{79/718} =
\log\frac{639}{79}$, and the minimum at the right endpoint, where it is
$\log\frac{0.88997213}{0.11002787} = \log\frac{88997213}{11002787}$. Apply
Lemma~\ref{lem:logs}. Formally one argues by monotonicity of $\log$ on each term
separately.
\end{proof}

The right endpoint $0.11002787$ is legitimate input: it is the certified upper
bound of the eight-decimal enclosure, so the hypothesis $\pstar < q_1$ of
Theorem~\ref{thm:newton} is already proved.

\section{Main results}

\begin{theorem}[Thirteen certified decimals]\label{thm:main}
Every $p \in [0,\tfrac12]$ with $r(p) = 0$ satisfies
\[
0.1100278644383 \;<\; p \;<\; 0.1100278644384 .
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Apply Theorem~\ref{thm:newton} with $q_0 = \frac{79}{718}$, $q_1 = 0.11002787$,
$A_1 = 1.941021565465\times10^{-8}$, $A_2 = 1.941021565843\times 10^{-8}$,
$L = 2.0904563381$ and $U = 2.0904568254$. The hypothesis $q_0 < p$ holds because
$79/718 = 0.1100278551\ldots$ lies below the certified lower bound $0.11002786$
of the eight-decimal enclosure; $p < q_1$ is that enclosure's upper bound. The
value bracket is Corollary~\ref{cor:anchorval} and the derivative bracket is
Theorem~\ref{thm:deriv}. Evaluating the two rational endpoints exactly,
\[
0.110027864438358347\ldots \;<\; p \;<\; 0.110027864438360514\ldots,
\]
an interval of width $2.166\times 10^{-15}$, contained in
$(0.1100278644383,\ 0.1100278644384)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}
$\lfloor 10^{13}\, \pstar \rfloor = 1100278644383$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{theorem}[Certified constant, unique]
There is exactly one real $p$ with $p \in [0,\tfrac12]$, $r(p) = 0$ and
$\lfloor 10^{13} p\rfloor = 1100278644383$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Certified error of the textbook value]
\[
2.786\times10^{-5} \;<\; \left|\pstar - \tfrac{11}{100}\right| \;<\; 2.787\times 10^{-5} .
\]
In particular $\pstar > 11/100$: quoting $11\%$ \emph{understates} the tolerable
error rate by $2.7864438\ldots\times 10^{-5}$ in absolute error rate, a relative
$2.53\times10^{-4}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{clcc}
\toprule
Stage & Method & Enclosure & Decimals \\
\midrule
--- & elementary bounds & $(0.0625,\ 0.125)$ & $0$ \\
$1$ & integer certificates at $b = 10^4$ & $(0.1100,\ 0.1101)$ & $4$ \\
$2$ & mean-value step, anchor $11/100$, crude $\log$ bounds & $(0.110027,\ 0.110029)$ & $6$ \\
$3$ & mean-value step, anchor $11/100$, Pad\'e bounds & $(0.11002786,\ 0.11002787)$ & $8$ \\
$4$ & mean-value step, anchor $79/718$, Pad\'e bounds & width $2.17\times10^{-15}$ & $13$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\section{Algorithms}

\subsection{Sign decision at a rational}
Given positive integers $a,c$, compute $D = (a+c)^{2(a+c)}$ and
$N = 2^{a+c}a^{2a}c^{2c}$ exactly and compare; correctness is
Theorem~\ref{thm:sign}. With binary powering and fast multiplication the cost is
$\tilde O(b\log b)$ bit operations for $b = a+c$; with naive repeated
multiplication it is $\Theta(b^2)$, the practical bottleneck in
exact-verification settings.

\subsection{Value bracket at a rational}
Given $a,c$ and a precision parameter $n = 10^{s}$, compute $N, D$, set
$m_- = \lfloor nN/D\rfloor$ and $m_+ = m_- + 1$, so $m_-D < nN < m_+D$. Then
\[
v_- = \frac{1}{a+c}\cdot\frac{2(m_-/n - 1)}{m_-/n + 1},
\qquad
v_+ = \frac{1}{a+c}\cdot\frac{m_+/n - n/m_+}{2}
\]
satisfy $v_- < r(a/(a+c)) < v_+$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:val}. The width is
$O\!\left(\frac{1}{(a+c)n}\right)$ plus the Pad\'e slack $O((N/D-1)^3)$.

\subsection{Continued-fraction anchor selection}
Run the Gauss map $x_0 = \pstar$, $a_k = \lfloor x_k\rfloor$,
$x_{k+1} = (x_k - a_k)^{-1}$, accumulating $p_k = a_kp_{k-1} + p_{k-2}$,
$q_k = a_kq_{k-1} + q_{k-2}$, and return the convergent of largest
$q_k \le Q_{\max}$; cost $O(\log Q_{\max})$ steps. The approximation used need
not be trusted: it only \emph{selects} the anchor, whose position is subsequently
certified.

\subsection{The full pipeline}
\begin{enumerate}
\item Select an anchor $q_0 = a/(a+c)$ within the arithmetic budget.
\item Certify $q_0 < \pstar$; take $q_1 > \pstar$ from the previous enclosure.
\item Certify $A_1 < \tfrac12 r(q_0) < A_2$.
\item Certify $L \le H_2' \le U$ on $[q_0,q_1]$ by monotonicity plus two
      logarithms of explicit rationals, splitting off the nearest power of $2$.
\item Output $\left(q_0 + \frac{A_1}{U},\ q_0 + \frac{A_2}{L}\right)$.
\end{enumerate}

\section{Cost analysis: the quartic law}

Let $q$ be the denominator of the anchor. The certificate integers have
$\Theta(q\log q)$ digits, so the comparison costs $\Theta(q^2)$ up to logarithmic
factors. A convergent of denominator $q$ has $\delta \asymp q^{-2}$ whenever the
partial quotients are bounded, and by Corollary~\ref{cor:quad} one mean-value
step yields width $\varepsilon \approx 4.9\,\delta^2 \approx q^{-4}$. Eliminating
$q$ gives $q \approx \varepsilon^{-1/4}$ and cost $\approx \varepsilon^{-1/2}$.
By contrast the pure arithmetic scheme needs $q \approx \varepsilon^{-1}$ and
cost $\varepsilon^{-2}$, and a decimal-anchored mean-value scheme needs
$q \approx \varepsilon^{-1/2}$ and cost $\varepsilon^{-1}$: the Diophantine
anchor halves the cost exponent twice.

Concretely, the four-decimal stage used $80\,000$-digit integers to reach
$\varepsilon = 10^{-4}$, while the thirteen-decimal stage used $4102$-digit
integers to reach $\varepsilon = 2\times10^{-15}$. Extrapolating with the next
convergent $16466/149653$ ($\delta \approx 2.1\times 10^{-11}$, certificate
integers of $\approx 1.6\times 10^{6}$ digits) would give
$\varepsilon \approx 2\times 10^{-21}$.

A secondary limit eventually binds: the derivative bracket inherits the accuracy
of the input bound on $\log 2$. With nine certified digits its contribution to
the final width is below $10^{-17}$, invisible at thirteen decimals but leading
somewhere around eighteen.

\section{Discussion}

\paragraph{What is actually certified.}
Every statement of Section~7 is a chain of implications from: the definition of
$H_2$; exact integer comparisons; the Pad\'e inequalities, proved from the sign of
an explicit derivative; the mean value theorem; and a two-sided rational bound on
$\log 2$. There is no interval arithmetic over floating point, no numerically
evaluated transcendental, and no step in which an approximation is silently
treated as exact. The high-precision value of $\pstar$ used to \emph{choose} the
anchor plays no logical role: had it been wrong, the anchor certificates would
simply have failed.

\paragraph{Why the anchor need not be assumed close.}
A frequent worry about Newton-type enclosures is circularity: one seems to need to
know where the root is in order to place the anchor. Theorem~\ref{thm:newton} has
no such hypothesis; it requires only $q_0 < p < q_1$ and the two brackets, each
certified independently. A badly chosen anchor produces a valid but wide
enclosure, never a false one.

\paragraph{Interpretation for quantum key distribution.}
First, the classical figure is safe but conservative: $11\%$ lies strictly below
$\pstar$, so any device certified at $Q \le 11\%$ genuinely produces key, with an
unused margin of $2.7864438\ldots\times 10^{-5}$. Second, the rate at $11\%$ is
now known quantitatively,
$r(0.11) = 1.16506723\ldots\times 10^{-4}$ nats per sifted bit --- roughly one
secret bit per $6000$ sifted bits. Third, finite-key and decoy-state analyses
that insert ``$0.11$'' for the threshold now carry a known, rather than unknown,
systematic offset.

\paragraph{Limitations.}
The rate function analysed here is the standard asymptotic one-way
collective-attack expression $\log 2 - 2H_2(Q)$. Two-way post-processing,
advantage distillation, finite-key corrections, imperfect sources and
device-independent settings have different rate functions and hence different
thresholds; the method transfers but the constant does not. The pipeline also
exploits the special structure of $H_2$ at rational arguments --- that
$\exp(2(a+c)H_2(a/(a+c)))$ is rational --- which is what makes the sign criterion
an exact integer comparison. Functions without this structure need a substitute
for Section~3, though Sections~4--6 apply unchanged once any certified value
bracket is available.

\section{Future directions}

\begin{conjecture}[Quartic certification law]
Let $f$ be real-analytic with a simple root $\pstar$ in an interval on which $f'$
is bounded away from $0$, and suppose the sign of $f$ at any rational $a/b$ is
decidable by an integer comparison of size $O(b\log b)$. Then a certified
enclosure of $\pstar$ of width $\varepsilon$ is obtainable at arithmetic cost
$O(\varepsilon^{-1/2})$, rather than $O(\varepsilon^{-1})$, by anchoring at
continued-fraction convergents of $\pstar$.
\end{conjecture}

\begin{conjecture}[Binary-powering certificates break the $b^2$ wall]
Replacing linearly-unfolded exponentiation by a verified binary-powering routine
makes the certificate at denominator $b = 10^6$ feasible, after which the pure
arithmetic scheme alone --- with no analysis --- certifies $\pstar$ to twelve
decimals. The obstruction to more decimals by brute force is a property of the
evaluator, not of the threshold.
\end{conjecture}

Further directions include: \emph{iterating the anchor}, using the
thirteen-decimal enclosure to select $16466/149653$ and reach $\approx 10^{-21}$;
\emph{second-order steps}, replacing the mean value theorem by a Taylor step with
a certified bound on $H_2''$, making the width cubic in $\delta$ and the cost
exponent $1/3$; a \emph{catalogue of certified information-theoretic constants}
(six-state protocol threshold, two-way post-processing thresholds, R\'enyi level
sets, capacity fixed points); \emph{certified $\log 2$} to arbitrary precision
from a series with explicit tail bound; and the question of \emph{anchor
optimality}, namely whether convergents are always the best anchors once the cost
of the certificate, rather than the denominator, is the metric.

\section{Conclusion}

The BB84 error-rate threshold is $\pstar = 0.1100278644383\ldots$, certified to
thirteen decimals with an interval of width $2.17\times 10^{-15}$. The
certification rests on an exact reduction of a transcendental comparison to an
integer comparison, cubic-accuracy Pad\'e bounds for the logarithm, and a single
mean-value step from a well-chosen anchor. The decisive idea is that the anchor
should be a continued-fraction convergent of the threshold rather than a decimal:
approximation quality, not arithmetic size, is the resource that buys precision,
and the two scale with different exponents. As a by-product, the textbook value
$11\%$ is revealed to be the best rational approximation of the threshold with
denominator below $309$ --- a coincidence which, on reflection, is no coincidence
at all.

"""
Certified enclosure of the BB84 quantum bit error rate threshold.
================================================================

The asymptotic one-way BB84 secret-key rate, in nats per sifted bit, is

    r(Q) = log 2 - 2 * H2(Q),      H2(p) = -p log p - (1-p) log(1-p).

It vanishes at a unique threshold p* in (0, 1/2), quoted in the literature as
"about 11%".  This script reproduces, in exact integer / exact rational
arithmetic wherever it matters, the full certification pipeline that pins

    0.1100278644383 < p* < 0.1100278644384,   floor(10^13 p*) = 1100278644383.

The four stages are:

  1. The Rational Sign Criterion.  For positive integers a, c,
         H2(a/(a+c)) < (log 2)/2   <=>   (a+c)^(2(a+c)) < 2^(a+c) a^(2a) c^(2c),
     an *exact equivalence* between a transcendental comparison and a comparison
     of two integers.  No logarithm is evaluated.

  2. Pade value certificates.  For x >= 1,
         2(x-1)/(x+1) <= log x <= (x - 1/x)/2,
     with cubic error.  Combined with the exact identity
         r(a/(a+c)) = (1/(a+c)) log(N/D),  N = 2^(a+c) a^(2a) c^(2c),
                                           D = (a+c)^(2(a+c)),
     a pair of integer comparisons yields a rational two-sided bracket on r.

  3. The mean-value refinement step.  A certified anchor value plus a certified
     derivative bracket L <= H2' <= U on [q0, q1] gives
         q0 + A1/U < p* < q0 + A2/L.
     The resulting width is ~ 4.9 * (anchor error)^2.

  4. Diophantine anchors.  Continued-fraction convergents of p* beat decimals:
     79/718 sits 9.29e-9 from the root with only 4102-digit certificates.

Everything below uses Python's exact `int` and `Fraction`; floating point is
used only to *print* results and to select (not to justify) the anchor.

Run:  python3 demo.py
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from decimal import Decimal, getcontext
from fractions import Fraction
from typing import Iterator, List, Tuple

getcontext().prec = 80

# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
# High-precision helpers (Decimal; used for reference values and printing)
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #


def dec_ln(x: Decimal) -> Decimal:
    """Natural logarithm at the ambient Decimal precision."""
    return x.ln()


def binary_entropy(p: Decimal) -> Decimal:
    """H2(p) = -p log p - (1-p) log(1-p), in nats."""
    if p <= 0 or p >= 1:
        return Decimal(0)
    return -p * dec_ln(p) - (1 - p) * dec_ln(1 - p)


def key_rate(q: Decimal) -> Decimal:
    """Asymptotic one-way BB84 secret-key rate r(Q) = log 2 - 2 H2(Q), in nats."""
    return Decimal(2).ln() - 2 * binary_entropy(q)


def reference_threshold(iterations: int = 400) -> Decimal:
    """High-precision p* by bisection.  Used only as a reference / anchor picker."""
    lo, hi = Decimal("0.05"), Decimal("0.15")
    for _ in range(iterations):
        mid = (lo + hi) / 2
        if key_rate(mid) > 0:
            lo = mid
        else:
            hi = mid
    return (lo + hi) / 2


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
# Stage 1: the Rational Sign Criterion (pure integer arithmetic)
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #


def certificate_pair(a: int, c: int) -> Tuple[int, int]:
    """Return the two certificate integers (D, N) for the rational a/(a+c),

        D = (a+c)^(2(a+c)),     N = 2^(a+c) * a^(2a) * c^(2c).
    """
    b = a + c
    d = b ** (2 * b)
    n = (2 ** b) * (a ** (2 * a)) * (c ** (2 * c))
    return d, n


def sign_of_key_rate(a: int, c: int) -> int:
    """Sign of r(a/(a+c)):  +1 below threshold, -1 above, 0 exactly on it.

    Correctness is the Rational Sign Criterion: r > 0 iff D < N.  This is an
    equivalence, so the returned sign is exact -- no rounding is involved.
    """
    d, n = certificate_pair(a, c)
    return (d < n) - (n < d)


def decimal_digits(m: int) -> int:
    """Number of decimal digits of a (possibly huge) positive integer."""
    if m == 0:
        return 1
    # log10(m) from the bit length, then corrected exactly by one comparison.
    approx = int(m.bit_length() * 0.30102999566398119802) + 1
    while 10 ** (approx - 1) > m:
        approx -= 1
    while 10 ** approx <= m:
        approx += 1
    return approx


def certificate_digits(a: int, c: int) -> int:
    """Number of decimal digits of the larger certificate integer."""
    d, n = certificate_pair(a, c)
    return decimal_digits(max(d, n))


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
# Stage 2: Pade bounds and value certificates
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #


def pade_lower(x: Fraction) -> Fraction:
    """2(x-1)/(x+1) <= log x for x >= 1."""
    return 2 * (x - 1) / (x + 1)


def pade_upper(x: Fraction) -> Fraction:
    """log x <= (x - 1/x)/2 for x >= 1."""
    return (x - 1 / x) / 2


def key_rate_bracket(a: int, c: int, digits: int = 20) -> Tuple[Fraction, Fraction]:
    """Certified rational bracket (v_lo, v_hi) with v_lo < r(a/(a+c)) < v_hi.

    Uses exact integers to round the ratio N/D to `digits` significant places
    from below and above, then applies the Pade bounds.  Valid only when the
    anchor is below threshold (D < N); otherwise the Pade hypotheses fail.
    """
    b = a + c
    d, n = certificate_pair(a, c)
    if not d < n:
        raise ValueError("anchor is not below threshold; Pade hypotheses need N >= D")
    scale = 10 ** digits
    m_lo = (scale * n) // d           # m_lo * D <= scale * N
    m_hi = m_lo + 1                   # scale * N <  m_hi * D
    r_lo = Fraction(m_lo, scale)
    r_hi = Fraction(m_hi, scale)
    return (pade_lower(r_lo) / b, pade_upper(r_hi) / b)


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
# Stage 3: the mean-value refinement step
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #


def refinement_step(
    q0: Fraction, a1: Fraction, a2: Fraction, low: Fraction, up: Fraction
) -> Tuple[Fraction, Fraction]:
    """One certified mean-value step.

    Hypotheses (all certified elsewhere):
        q0 < p* < q1,
        a1 < r(q0)/2 < a2,
        low <= H2'(x) <= up  for all x in [q0, q1],  low > 0.
    Conclusion:
        q0 + a1/up < p* < q0 + a2/low.
    """
    if low <= 0:
        raise ValueError("derivative lower bound must be positive")
    return (q0 + a1 / up, q0 + a2 / low)


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
# Stage 4: continued-fraction anchors
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #


def continued_fraction(x: Fraction, terms: int) -> List[int]:
    """Partial quotients [a0; a1, a2, ...] of the rational x."""
    out: List[int] = []
    y = x
    for _ in range(terms):
        a = y.numerator // y.denominator
        out.append(a)
        y -= a
        if y == 0:
            break
        y = 1 / y
    return out


def convergents(quotients: List[int]) -> Iterator[Fraction]:
    """Convergents p_k/q_k from the partial quotients, by the standard recurrence."""
    p_prev, p_cur = 0, 1
    q_prev, q_cur = 1, 0
    for a in quotients:
        p_prev, p_cur = p_cur, a * p_cur + p_prev
        q_prev, q_cur = q_cur, a * q_cur + q_prev
        yield Fraction(p_cur, q_cur)


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
# The demonstration
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #


def rule(title: str) -> None:
    print("\n" + "=" * 74)
    print(title)
    print("=" * 74)


def main() -> None:
    p_ref = reference_threshold()

    rule("0.  The constant")
    print(f"  reference p*            = {str(p_ref)[:34]}...")
    print(f"  H2(p*)                  = {str(binary_entropy(p_ref))[:24]}...")
    print(f"  (log 2)/2               = {str(Decimal(2).ln() / 2)[:24]}...")
    print(f"  r(p*)  (should be ~0)   = {key_rate(p_ref):.3e}")
    print(f"  H2'(p*) = log((1-p)/p)  = {dec_ln(1 - p_ref) - dec_ln(p_ref)}"[:60])

    rule("1.  The Rational Sign Criterion  (exact integer comparisons)")
    print("     H2(a/(a+c)) < (log 2)/2   <=>   (a+c)^(2(a+c)) < 2^(a+c) a^(2a) c^(2c)")
    print()
    print(f"  {'rational':>16} {'value':>14} {'digits':>8} {'verdict':>16}")
    for a, c in [(1, 15), (1, 7), (11, 89), (34, 275), (79, 639), (1101, 8899)]:
        s = sign_of_key_rate(a, c)
        verdict = {1: "below threshold", -1: "above threshold", 0: "exactly on"}[s]
        print(
            f"  {f'{a}/{a + c}':>16} {a / (a + c):>14.10f} "
            f"{certificate_digits(a, c):>8} {verdict:>16}"
        )
    print()
    print("  Note 1/16 = 0.0625 is below and 1/8 = 0.125 is above: the coarse bracket.")
    print("  11/100 is below and 1101/10000 above: four certified decimals,")
    print("  but the latter needs 80000-digit integers.  This is the brute-force wall.")

    rule("2.  Pade bounds for the logarithm  (cubic accuracy near 1)")
    print("     2(x-1)/(x+1) <= log x <= (x - 1/x)/2      for x >= 1")
    print()
    print(f"  {'x':>12} {'lower':>22} {'log x':>22} {'upper':>22}")
    for xs in ["1.0000279", "1.011", "1.1", "2.0"]:
        xf = Fraction(xs)
        lo = float(pade_lower(xf))
        hi = float(pade_upper(xf))
        mid = float(Decimal(xs).ln())
        print(f"  {xs:>12} {lo:>22.16f} {mid:>22.16f} {hi:>22.16f}")
    print()
    print("  Relative slack at x = 1.0000279 is ~7e-15: the reason 13 decimals fit.")

    rule("3.  Continued fraction of the threshold  (Diophantine anchors)")
    quots = continued_fraction(Fraction(str(p_ref)), 8)
    print(f"  p* = {quots[:1]} ; {quots[1:]}   (partial quotients)")
    print()
    print(f"  {'k':>3} {'convergent':>18} {'decimal':>18} {'error':>13} {'cert digits':>12}")
    for k, cv in enumerate(convergents(quots)):
        err = float(Decimal(cv.numerator) / Decimal(cv.denominator) - p_ref)
        digits = ""
        if 0 < cv.denominator <= 800 and cv.numerator > 0:
            digits = str(certificate_digits(cv.numerator, cv.denominator - cv.numerator))
        print(
            f"  {k:>3} {f'{cv.numerator}/{cv.denominator}':>18} "
            f"{float(cv):>18.13f} {err:>13.3e} {digits:>12}"
        )
    print()
    print("  11/100 is the convergent k=2, and q_3 = 309: so 11/100 is the BEST")
    print("  rational approximation of p* with denominator <= 308.  The textbook")
    print("  value is optimal for its size -- not a lazy rounding.")
    print()
    print("  79/718 (k=4) is 3000x closer to p* than 11/100, yet its certificate")
    print("  has only 4102 digits versus 80000 for the four-decimal stage.")

    rule("4.  Certified key rate at the anchor 79/718")
    a, c = 79, 639
    d, n = certificate_pair(a, c)
    print(f"  D = 718^1436                          ({decimal_digits(d)} digits)")
    print(f"  N = 2^718 * 79^158 * 639^1278         ({decimal_digits(n)} digits)")
    print(f"  D < N ?  {d < n}   -> the anchor is strictly below threshold")
    print()
    lo_int = 100002787345813950188
    hi_int = 100002787345813950189
    print("  Integer certificates pinning N/D to twenty significant figures:")
    print(f"    {lo_int} * D  <  10^20 * N   :  {lo_int * d < 10**20 * n}")
    print(f"    10^20 * N  <  {hi_int} * D   :  {10**20 * n < hi_int * d}")
    print(f"    N/D = {Decimal(n) / Decimal(d)}"[:60])
    print()
    v_lo, v_hi = key_rate_bracket(a, c, digits=20)
    print(f"  Certified:  {float(v_lo):.15e} < r(79/718) < {float(v_hi):.15e}")
    print(f"  Exact:      r(79/718) = {key_rate(Decimal(a) / Decimal(a + c)):.15e}")
    print(f"  Bracket contains the true value: {v_lo < Fraction(str(key_rate(Decimal(a) / Decimal(a + c)))) < v_hi}")

    rule("5.  The derivative bracket on [79/718, 0.11002787]")
    q0 = Fraction(79, 718)
    q1 = Fraction(11002787, 100000000)
    left = dec_ln(1 - Decimal(q0.numerator) / Decimal(q0.denominator)) - dec_ln(

demos.name: End-to-End Certification of the BB84 Threshold: From Integer Certificates to Thirteen Decimals
demos.description: A single self-contained script that walks the entire certification pipeline in exact arithmetic. It (i) locates the threshold to high precision as a reference value; (ii) applies the Rational Sign Criterion to a family of rational error rates, printing the exact verdict and the size of the certificate integers involved; (iii) tabulates the Pade bounds for the logarithm against the true value at several arguments, showing their cubic accuracy near 1; (iv) computes the continued fraction of the threshold and its convergents, exhibiting 11/100 as a convergent and 79/718 as the anchor of choice; (v) verifies the twenty-digit integer certificates for 79/718 and derives the certified key-rate bracket there; (vi) checks the derivative bracket on the interval between the anchor and the barrier; (vii) executes the mean-value step and confirms that the resulting interval has width 2.17e-15 and pins floor(10^13 p*) = 1100278644383; and (viii) prints the certified error of the textbook value 11% together with a table illustrating the quartic cost-versus-precision law.
demos.code:
"""
Certified enclosure of the BB84 quantum bit error rate threshold.
================================================================

The asymptotic one-way BB84 secret-key rate, in nats per sifted bit, is

    r(Q) = log 2 - 2 * H2(Q),      H2(p) = -p log p - (1-p) log(1-p).

It vanishes at a unique threshold p* in (0, 1/2), quoted in the literature as
"about 11%".  This script reproduces, in exact integer / exact rational
arithmetic wherever it matters, the full certification pipeline that pins

    0.1100278644383 < p* < 0.1100278644384,   floor(10^13 p*) = 1100278644383.

The four stages are:

  1. The Rational Sign Criterion.  For positive integers a, c,
         H2(a/(a+c)) < (log 2)/2   <=>   (a+c)^(2(a+c)) < 2^(a+c) a^(2a) c^(2c),
     an *exact equivalence* between a transcendental comparison and a comparison
     of two integers.  No logarithm is evaluated.

  2. Pade value certificates.  For x >= 1,
         2(x-1)/(x+1) <= log x <= (x - 1/x)/2,
     with cubic error.  Combined with the exact identity
         r(a/(a+c)) = (1/(a+c)) log(N/D),  N = 2^(a+c) a^(2a) c^(2c),
                                           D = (a+c)^(2(a+c)),
     a pair of integer comparisons yields a rational two-sided bracket on r.

  3. The mean-value refinement step.  A certified anchor value plus a certified
     derivative bracket L <= H2' <= U on [q0, q1] gives
         q0 + A1/U < p* < q0 + A2/L.
     The resulting width is ~ 4.9 * (anchor error)^2.

  4. Diophantine anchors.  Continued-fraction convergents of p* beat decimals:
     79/718 sits 9.29e-9 from the root with only 4102-digit certificates.

Everything below uses Python's exact `int` and `Fraction`; floating point is
used only to *print* results and to select (not to justify) the anchor.

Run:  python3 demo.py
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from decimal import Decimal, getcontext
from fractions import Fraction
from typing import Iterator, List, Tuple

getcontext().prec = 80

# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
# High-precision helpers (Decimal; used for reference values and printing)
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #


def dec_ln(x: Decimal) -> Decimal:
    """Natural logarithm at the ambient Decimal precision."""
    return x.ln()


def binary_entropy(p: Decimal) -> Decimal:
    """H2(p) = -p log p - (1-p) log(1-p), in nats."""
    if p <= 0 or p >= 1:
        return Decimal(0)
    return -p * dec_ln(p) - (1 - p) * dec_ln(1 - p)


def key_rate(q: Decimal) -> Decimal:
    """Asymptotic one-way BB84 secret-key rate r(Q) = log 2 - 2 H2(Q), in nats."""
    return Decimal(2).ln() - 2 * binary_entropy(q)


def reference_threshold(iterations: int = 400) -> Decimal:
    """High-precision p* by bisection.  Used only as a reference / anchor picker."""
    lo, hi = Decimal("0.05"), Decimal("0.15")
    for _ in range(iterations):
        mid = (lo + hi) / 2
        if key_rate(mid) > 0:
            lo = mid
        else:
            hi = mid
    return (lo + hi) / 2


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
# Stage 1: the Rational Sign Criterion (pure integer arithmetic)
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #


def certificate_pair(a: int, c: int) -> Tuple[int, int]:
    """Return the two certificate integers (D, N) for the rational a/(a+c),

        D = (a+c)^(2(a+c)),     N = 2^(a+c) * a^(2a) * c^(2c).
    """
    b = a + c
    d = b ** (2 * b)
    n = (2 ** b) * (a ** (2 * a)) * (c ** (2 * c))
    return d, n


def sign_of_key_rate(a: int, c: int) -> int:
    """Sign of r(a/(a+c)):  +1 below threshold, -1 above, 0 exactly on it.

    Correctness is the Rational Sign Criterion: r > 0 iff D < N.  This is an
    equivalence, so the returned sign is exact -- no rounding is involved.
    """
    d, n = certificate_pair(a, c)
    return (d < n) - (n < d)


def decimal_digits(m: int) -> int:
    """Number of decimal digits of a (possibly huge) positive integer."""
    if m == 0:
        return 1
    # log10(m) from the bit length, then corrected exactly by one comparison.
    approx = int(m.bit_length() * 0.30102999566398119802) + 1
    while 10 ** (approx - 1) > m:
        approx -= 1
    while 10 ** approx <= m:
        approx += 1
    return approx


def certificate_digits(a: int, c: int) -> int:
    """Number of decimal digits of the larger certificate integer."""
    d, n = certificate_pair(a, c)
    return decimal_digits(max(d, n))


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
# Stage 2: Pade bounds and value certificates
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #


def pade_lower(x: Fraction) -> Fraction:
    """2(x-1)/(x+1) <= log x for x >= 1."""
    return 2 * (x - 1) / (x + 1)


def pade_upper(x: Fraction) -> Fraction:
    """log x <= (x - 1/x)/2 for x >= 1."""
    return (x - 1 / x) / 2


def key_rate_bracket(a: int, c: int, digits: int = 20) -> Tuple[Fraction, Fraction]:
    """Certified rational bracket (v_lo, v_hi) with v_lo < r(a/(a+c)) < v_hi.

    Uses exact integers to round the ratio N/D to `digits` significant places
    from below and above, then applies the Pade bounds.  Valid only when the
    anchor is below threshold (D < N); otherwise the Pade hypotheses fail.
    """
    b = a + c
    d, n = certificate_pair(a, c)
    if not d < n:
        raise ValueError("anchor is not below threshold; Pade hypotheses need N >= D")
    scale = 10 ** digits
    m_lo = (scale * n) // d           # m_lo * D <= scale * N
    m_hi = m_lo + 1                   # scale * N <  m_hi * D
    r_lo = Fraction(m_lo, scale)
    r_hi = Fraction(m_hi, scale)
    return (pade_lower(r_lo) / b, pade_upper(r_hi) / b)


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
# Stage 3: the mean-value refinement step
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #


def refinement_step(
    q0: Fraction, a1: Fraction, a2: Fraction, low: Fraction, up: Fraction
) -> Tuple[Fraction, Fraction]:
    """One certified mean-value step.

    Hypotheses (all certified elsewhere):
        q0 < p* < q1,
        a1 < r(q0)/2 < a2,
        low <= H2'(x) <= up  for all x in [q0, q1],  low > 0.
    Conclusion:
        q0 + a1/up < p* < q0 + a2/low.
    """
    if low <= 0:
        raise ValueError("derivative lower bound must be positive")
    return (q0 + a1 / up, q0 + a2 / low)


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
# Stage 4: continued-fraction anchors
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #


def continued_fraction(x: Fraction, terms: int) -> List[int]:
    """Partial quotients [a0; a1, a2, ...] of the rational x."""
    out: List[int] = []
    y = x
    for _ in range(terms):
        a = y.numerator // y.denominator
        out.append(a)
        y -= a
        if y == 0:
            break
        y = 1 / y
    return out


def convergents(quotients: List[int]) -> Iterator[Fraction]:
    """Convergents p_k/q_k from the partial quotients, by the standard recurrence."""
    p_prev, p_cur = 0, 1
    q_prev, q_cur = 1, 0
    for a in quotients:
        p_prev, p_cur = p_cur, a * p_cur + p_prev
        q_prev, q_cur = q_cur, a * q_cur + q_prev
        yield Fraction(p_cur, q_cur)


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
# The demonstration
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #


def rule(title: str) -> None:
    print("\n" + "=" * 74)
    print(title)
    print("=" * 74)


def main() -> None:
    p_ref = reference_threshold()

    rule("0.  The constant")
    print(f"  reference p*            = {str(p_ref)[:34]}...")
    print(f"  H2(p*)                  = {str(binary_entropy(p_ref))[:24]}...")
    print(f"  (log 2)/2               = {str(Decimal(2).ln() / 2)[:24]}...")
    print(f"  r(p*)  (should be ~0)   = {key_rate(p_ref):.3e}")
    print(f"  H2'(p*) = log((1-p)/p)  = {dec_ln(1 - p_ref) - dec_ln(p_ref)}"[:60])

    rule("1.  The Rational Sign Criterion  (exact integer comparisons)")
    print("     H2(a/(a+c)) < (log 2)/2   <=>   (a+c)^(2(a+c)) < 2^(a+c) a^(2a) c^(2c)")
    print()
    print(f"  {'rational':>16} {'value':>14} {'digits':>8} {'verdict':>16}")
    for a, c in [(1, 15), (1, 7), (11, 89), (34, 275), (79, 639), (1101, 8899)]:
        s = sign_of_key_rate(a, c)
        verdict = {1: "below threshold", -1: "above threshold", 0: "exactly on"}[s]
        print(
            f"  {f'{a}/{a + c}':>16} {a / (a + c):>14.10f} "
            f"{certificate_digits(a, c):>8} {verdict:>16}"
        )
    print()
    print("  Note 1/16 = 0.0625 is below and 1/8 = 0.125 is above: the coarse bracket.")
    print("  11/100 is below and 1101/10000 above: four certified decimals,")
    print("  but the latter needs 80000-digit integers.  This is the brute-force wall.")

    rule("2.  Pade bounds for the logarithm  (cubic accuracy near 1)")
    print("     2(x-1)/(x+1) <= log x <= (x - 1/x)/2      for x >= 1")
    print()
    print(f"  {'x':>12} {'lower':>22} {'log x':>22} {'upper':>22}")
    for xs in ["1.0000279", "1.011", "1.1", "2.0"]:
        xf = Fraction(xs)
        lo = float(pade_lower(xf))
        hi = float(pade_upper(xf))
        mid = float(Decimal(xs).ln())
        print(f"  {xs:>12} {lo:>22.16f} {mid:>22.16f} {hi:>22.16f}")
    print()
    print("  Relative slack at x = 1.0000279 is ~7e-15: the reason 13 decimals fit.")

    rule("3.  Continued fraction of the threshold  (Diophantine anchors)")
    quots = continued_fraction(Fraction(str(p_ref)), 8)
    print(f"  p* = {quots[:1]} ; {quots[1:]}   (partial quotients)")
    print()
    print(f"  {'k':>3} {'convergent':>18} {'decimal':>18} {'error':>13} {'cert digits':>12}")
    for k, cv in enumerate(convergents(quots)):
        err = float(Decimal(cv.numerator) / Decimal(cv.denominator) - p_ref)
        digits = ""
        if 0 < cv.denominator <= 800 and cv.numerator > 0:

        print(
            f"  {k:>3} {f'{cv.numerator}/{cv.denominator}':>18} "
            f"{float(cv):>18.13f} {err:>13.3e} {digits:>12}"
        )
    print()
    print("  11/100 is the convergent k=2, and q_3 = 309: so 11/100 is the BEST")
    print("  rational approximation of p* with denominator <= 308.  The textbook")
    print("  value is optimal for its size -- not a lazy rounding.")
    print()
    print("  79/718 (k=4) is 3000x closer to p* than 11/100, yet its certificate")
    print("  has only 4102 digits versus 80000 for the four-decimal stage.")

    rule("4.  Certified key rate at the anchor 79/718")
    a, c = 79, 639
    d, n = certificate_pair(a, c)
    print(f"  D = 718^1436                          ({decimal_digits(d)} digits)")
    print(f"  N = 2^718 * 79^158 * 639^1278         ({decimal_digits(n)} digits)")
    print(f"  D < N ?  {d < n}   -> the anchor is strictly below threshold")
    print()
    lo_int = 100002787345813950188
    hi_int = 100002787345813950189
    print("  Integer certificates pinning N/D to twenty significant figures:")
    print(f"    {lo_int} * D  <  10^20 * N   :  {lo_int * d < 10**20 * n}")

    print()

    print(f"  Bracket contains the true value: {v_lo < Fraction(str(key_rate(Decimal(a) / Decimal(a + c)))) < v_hi}")

    rule("5.  The derivative bracket on [79/718, 0.11002787]")
    q0 = Fraction(79, 718)
    q1 = Fraction(11002787, 100000000)
    left = dec_ln(1 - Decimal(q0.numerator) / Decimal(q0.denominator)) - dec_ln(

    print(f"    min at x = 0.11002787    : log(88997213/11002787) = {str(right)[:16]}")
    print(f"  Certified bracket           : [{float(L):.10f}, {float(U):.10f}]")

    print(f"  Bracket width               : {float(U - L):.4e}")

algorithms.name: The Rational Sign Criterion: Exact Integer Decision of Threshold Position
algorithms.description: Decides, exactly, whether a rational quantum bit error rate a/(a+c) lies below or above the BB84 threshold, without evaluating any transcendental function. The identity 2(a+c)H2(a/(a+c)) = 2(a+c)log(a+c) - 2a log a - 2c log c has integer coefficients on every logarithm, so exponentiating the comparison against (a+c)log 2 turns it into the integer comparison D = (a+c)^(2(a+c)) versus N = 2^(a+c) a^(2a) c^(2c). Because this is an equivalence rather than a bound, the procedure is a complete decision procedure. The certificate integers have Theta(b log b) decimal digits for b = a+c; with binary powering and fast multiplication the cost is quasi-linear in that size, while naive repeated multiplication gives Theta(b^2). Binary searching over numerators certifies a decimal enclosure at cost O(log b) probes, which is practical up to b around 10^4.
algorithms.pseudocode:
function SIGN-OF-KEY-RATE(a, c):
    require a > 0 and c > 0
    b <- a + c
    D <- b^(2b)                      # exact integer
    N <- 2^b * a^(2a) * c^(2c)       # exact integer
    if D < N: return +1              # r(a/b) > 0, below threshold
    if N < D: return -1              # r(a/b) < 0, above threshold
    return 0                         # exactly on the threshold

function BISECT-THRESHOLD(b):
    lo <- 0 ; hi <- floor(b/2)
    while hi - lo > 1:
        mid <- floor((lo + hi)/2)
        if SIGN-OF-KEY-RATE(mid, b - mid) > 0:
            lo <- mid                # mid/b still below threshold
        else:
            hi <- mid
    return (lo, hi)                  # lo/b < p* < hi/b, hi = lo + 1
algorithms.code:
"""Algorithm 1 — The Rational Sign Criterion.

Decides, exactly and with no evaluation of any transcendental function, on which
side of the BB84 threshold a given rational error rate lies.

    H2(a/(a+c)) < (log 2)/2   <=>   (a+c)^(2(a+c)) < 2^(a+c) * a^(2a) * c^(2c)

The equivalence follows from the identity
    2(a+c) H2(a/(a+c)) = 2(a+c) log(a+c) - 2a log a - 2c log c
by exponentiation: every logarithm has an integer coefficient, so the comparison
of reals becomes a comparison of two integers.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import Literal, Tuple

Verdict = Literal["below", "above", "on"]


def certificate_pair(a: int, c: int) -> Tuple[int, int]:
    """Return (D, N) = ((a+c)^(2(a+c)), 2^(a+c) a^(2a) c^(2c)) as exact integers."""
    if a <= 0 or c <= 0:
        raise ValueError("a and c must be positive integers")
    b = a + c
    return b ** (2 * b), (2 ** b) * (a ** (2 * a)) * (c ** (2 * c))


def sign_of_key_rate(a: int, c: int) -> int:
    """+1 if r(a/(a+c)) > 0, -1 if r < 0, 0 if r = 0.  Exact."""
    d, n = certificate_pair(a, c)
    return (d < n) - (n < d)


def classify(a: int, c: int) -> Verdict:
    """Human-readable verdict for the rational error rate a/(a+c)."""
    s = sign_of_key_rate(a, c)
    return "below" if s > 0 else ("above" if s < 0 else "on")


def bisect_threshold(denominator: int) -> Tuple[int, int]:
    """Certified enclosure of p* with the given denominator, by binary search.

    Returns (lo, hi) with lo/denominator < p* < hi/denominator and hi = lo + 1.
    Each probe is one exact integer comparison.  Cost is
    O(log denominator) probes, each of cost Theta(denominator^2) with schoolbook
    arithmetic -- which is why this loop is only practical up to ~10^4.
    """
    lo, hi = 0, denominator // 2
    while hi - lo > 1:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if sign_of_key_rate(mid, denominator - mid) > 0:
            lo = mid
        else:
            hi = mid
    return lo, hi


if __name__ == "__main__":
    for a, c in [(1, 15), (1, 7), (11, 89), (34, 275), (79, 639)]:
        print(f"{a}/{a + c} = {a / (a + c):.10f}  ->  {classify(a, c)} threshold")
    print("enclosure at denominator 1000:", bisect_threshold(1000))

algorithms.name: Pade Value Certificates and the Certified Derivative Bracket
algorithms.description: Upgrades the sign criterion from a yes/no verdict to a certified numerical value. The key rate at a rational point is exactly r(a/(a+c)) = log(N/D)/(a+c), so certified numerics for r reduce to certified numerics for the logarithm near 1. The order-(1,1) Pade bounds 2(x-1)/(x+1) <= log x <= (x - 1/x)/2 for x >= 1 have error cubic in x-1 (against quadratic for the elementary bounds 1 - 1/x <= log x <= x - 1), and are proved in one line from the non-negativity of (x-1)^2/(x(x+1)^2) and (x-1)^2/(2x^2). Truncating N/D to s significant digits from below and above is exactly a pair of integer certificates, and monotonicity of both Pade expressions transports them to a rational bracket on r whose width is O(1/((a+c) 10^s)) plus the cubic Pade slack. The same machinery, applied after splitting off the nearest power of two, brackets the derivative H2'(x) = log((1-x)/x) on an interval by its two endpoint values. Cost: one big-integer division on top of the certificate pair.
algorithms.pseudocode:
function KEY-RATE-BRACKET(a, c, s):
    b <- a + c
    (D, N) <- CERTIFICATE-PAIR(a, c)
    require D < N                       # anchor below threshold
    scale <- 10^s
    m_lo <- floor(scale * N / D)        # m_lo * D <= scale * N
    m_hi <- m_lo + 1                    # scale * N <  m_hi * D
    v_lo <- (1/b) * 2*(m_lo/scale - 1)/(m_lo/scale + 1)
    v_hi <- (1/b) * (m_hi/scale - scale/m_hi)/2
    return (v_lo, v_hi)                 # v_lo < r(a/b) < v_hi

function BRACKET-LOG(x):                # certified two-sided bound, x >= 1
    k <- 0 ; y <- x
    while y >= 2: y <- y/2 ; k <- k+1   # split off 2^k
    lo <- k*LOG2_LOWER + 2*(y-1)/(y+1)
    hi <- k*LOG2_UPPER + (y - 1/y)/2
    return (lo, hi)

function DERIVATIVE-BRACKET(q0, q1):    # H2' on [q0, q1], H2' decreasing
    (L, _) <- BRACKET-LOG((1 - q1)/q1)  # minimum, at the right endpoint
    (_, U) <- BRACKET-LOG((1 - q0)/q0)  # maximum, at the left endpoint
    return (L, U)
algorithms.code:
"""Algorithm 2 — Pade value certificates for the secret-key rate.

The key rate at a rational error rate is exactly a scaled logarithm of a
rational number,

    r(a/(a+c)) = (1/(a+c)) * log(N/D),
    N = 2^(a+c) a^(2a) c^(2c),   D = (a+c)^(2(a+c)),

so certified numerics for r reduce to certified numerics for log near 1.  The
Pade bounds of order (1,1),

    2(x-1)/(x+1) <= log x <= (x - 1/x)/2        (x >= 1),

have error Theta((x-1)^3), against Theta((x-1)^2) for the elementary bounds
1 - 1/x <= log x <= x - 1.  Truncating N/D to s significant digits from below
and above turns the two Pade bounds into an exact rational bracket for r.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from fractions import Fraction
from typing import Tuple


def certificate_pair(a: int, c: int) -> Tuple[int, int]:
    """(D, N) as exact integers."""
    b = a + c
    return b ** (2 * b), (2 ** b) * (a ** (2 * a)) * (c ** (2 * c))


def pade_lower(x: Fraction) -> Fraction:
    """2(x-1)/(x+1) <= log x, valid for x >= 1."""
    if x < 1:
        raise ValueError("Pade lower bound requires x >= 1")
    return 2 * (x - 1) / (x + 1)


def pade_upper(x: Fraction) -> Fraction:
    """log x <= (x - 1/x)/2, valid for x >= 1."""
    if x < 1:
        raise ValueError("Pade upper bound requires x >= 1")
    return (x - 1 / x) / 2


def key_rate_bracket(a: int, c: int, sig_digits: int = 20) -> Tuple[Fraction, Fraction]:
    """Certified rational bracket (v_lo, v_hi) with v_lo < r(a/(a+c)) < v_hi.

    Requires the anchor to be below threshold (D < N).  The two truncations
        m_lo = floor(10^s N / D),  m_hi = m_lo + 1
    are exactly the integer certificates
        m_lo * D < 10^s * N < m_hi * D,
    and monotonicity of both Pade bounds transports them to the value of r.
    Cost: one exact big-integer division on top of the certificate pair.
    """
    b = a + c
    d, n = certificate_pair(a, c)
    if d >= n:
        raise ValueError("anchor must lie strictly below threshold")
    scale = 10 ** sig_digits
    m_lo = (scale * n) // d
    m_hi = m_lo + 1
    return (pade_lower(Fraction(m_lo, scale)) / b,
            pade_upper(Fraction(m_hi, scale)) / b)


def derivative_bracket(lo: Fraction, hi: Fraction, sig_digits: int = 20
                       ) -> Tuple[Fraction, Fraction]:
    """Certified bracket for H2'(x) = log((1-x)/x) on [lo, hi], from Pade bounds.

    H2' is strictly decreasing, so it suffices to bound
        U >= log((1-lo)/lo)   and   L <= log((1-hi)/hi).
    Each argument is close to a power of two; splitting off 2^k reduces the task
    to a logarithm of a ratio within ~1% of 1, where the Pade bounds are sharp.
    A certified two-sided rational bound on log 2 must be supplied.
    """
    log2_lo = Fraction(6931471803, 10 ** 10)
    log2_hi = Fraction(6931471808, 10 ** 10)

    def bracket_log(x: Fraction) -> Tuple[Fraction, Fraction]:
        k = 0
        y = x
        while y >= 2:
            y /= 2
            k += 1
        # now 1 <= y < 2; y is within a few percent of 1 in our applications
        return (k * log2_lo + pade_lower(y), k * log2_hi + pade_upper(y))

    _, upper = bracket_log((1 - lo) / lo)
    lower, _ = bracket_log((1 - hi) / hi)
    return (lower, upper)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    v_lo, v_hi = key_rate_bracket(79, 639, 20)
    print(f"r(79/718) in ({float(v_lo):.15e}, {float(v_hi):.15e})")
    L, U = derivative_bracket(Fraction(79, 718), Fraction(11002787, 10 ** 8))
    print(f"H2' on [79/718, 0.11002787] in [{float(L):.10f}, {float(U):.10f}]")

algorithms.name: Diophantine Anchor Selection and the Complete Enclosure Pipeline
algorithms.description: Selects the anchor and runs the whole certification. The governing law is that one mean-value step converts an anchor at distance delta from the root into an enclosure of width approximately 4.9 delta^2, while the certificate at denominator q costs about q^2. Continued-fraction convergents are, by the best-approximation theorem, the rationals that minimise delta for a given denominator, and they achieve delta of order q^-2; hence precision of order q^-4 at cost q^2, so an enclosure of width eps costs O(eps^(-1/2)) rather than O(eps^(-1)). Convergent selection runs the Gauss map and the standard recurrences in O(log Q_max) steps. Crucially, the high-precision value used to select the anchor carries no logical weight: the anchor's position and value are certified afterwards by exact integer comparisons, so a poor selection yields a wide enclosure but never a false one. The pipeline then certifies the anchor's position, its key-rate value, the derivative bracket, and applies the mean-value step.
algorithms.pseudocode:
function BEST-ANCHOR(target, Q_max):
    (p_prev, p_cur) <- (0, 1) ; (q_prev, q_cur) <- (1, 0)
    x <- target ; best <- 0
    repeat:
        a <- floor(x)
        (p_prev, p_cur) <- (p_cur, a*p_cur + p_prev)
        (q_prev, q_cur) <- (q_cur, a*q_cur + q_prev)
        if q_cur > Q_max: break
        best <- p_cur / q_cur
        if x = a: break
        x <- 1/(x - a)
    return best

function CERTIFY(anchor q0 = a/b, barrier q1, s):
    # 1. position
    require SIGN-OF-KEY-RATE(a, b - a) = +1        # q0 < p*
    #    q1 > p* is inherited from the previous stage
    # 2. value at the anchor
    (v_lo, v_hi) <- KEY-RATE-BRACKET(a, b - a, s)
    (A1, A2) <- (v_lo/2, v_hi/2)
    # 3. derivative bracket
    (L, U) <- DERIVATIVE-BRACKET(q0, q1)
    require L > 0
    # 4. one mean value step
    return (q0 + A1/U, q0 + A2/L)                  # certified enclosure of p*
algorithms.code:
"""Algorithm 3 — Diophantine anchor selection and the full certification pipeline.

The width of the enclosure produced by one mean-value step is ~ 4.9 * delta^2,
where delta is the distance from the anchor to the root, while the cost of the
anchor's certificate grows like q^2 in its denominator q.  Continued-fraction
convergents deliver delta ~ q^-2, so precision ~ q^-4 against cost ~ q^2: to
reach width eps costs ~ eps^{-1/2}, not eps^{-1}.

This module selects the best convergent within a denominator budget, then runs
the pipeline:  certify the anchor's position, certify its value, certify the
derivative bracket, take one mean-value step.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from decimal import Decimal, getcontext
from fractions import Fraction
from typing import Iterator, List, Tuple

getcontext().prec = 60


# ----------------------------------------------------------------- anchors --
def continued_fraction(x: Fraction, terms: int) -> List[int]:
    """Partial quotients of x."""
    out: List[int] = []
    y = x
    for _ in range(terms):
        a = y.numerator // y.denominator
        out.append(a)
        y -= a
        if y == 0:
            break
        y = 1 / y
    return out


def convergents(quotients: List[int]) -> Iterator[Fraction]:
    """Convergents p_k/q_k via p_k = a_k p_{k-1} + p_{k-2}, likewise for q_k."""
    p_prev, p_cur, q_prev, q_cur = 0, 1, 1, 0
    for a in quotients:
        p_prev, p_cur = p_cur, a * p_cur + p_prev
        q_prev, q_cur = q_cur, a * q_cur + q_prev
        yield Fraction(p_cur, q_cur)


def best_anchor(target: Fraction, max_denominator: int) -> Fraction:
    """Best rational approximation of `target` with denominator <= budget.

    By the classical best-approximation theorem this is the last convergent
    whose denominator fits the budget.  Cost O(log budget).  The target need
    only be an *approximation* of the root: the anchor's position is certified
    afterwards, so an inaccurate target yields a wide -- never a wrong -- result.
    """
    best = Fraction(0)
    for cv in convergents(continued_fraction(target, 30)):
        if cv.denominator > max_denominator:
            break
        best = cv
    return best


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- pipeline --
def certificate_pair(a: int, c: int) -> Tuple[int, int]:
    b = a + c
    return b ** (2 * b), (2 ** b) * (a ** (2 * a)) * (c ** (2 * c))


def pade_lower(x: Fraction) -> Fraction:
    return 2 * (x - 1) / (x + 1)


def pade_upper(x: Fraction) -> Fraction:
    return (x - 1 / x) / 2


def bracket_log(x: Fraction) -> Tuple[Fraction, Fraction]:
    """Certified two-sided bound on log x for x >= 1, by splitting off 2^k."""
    log2_lo = Fraction(6931471803, 10 ** 10)
    log2_hi = Fraction(6931471808, 10 ** 10)
    k, y = 0, x
    while y >= 2:
        y /= 2
        k += 1
    return (k * log2_lo + pade_lower(y), k * log2_hi + pade_upper(y))


def refinement_step(q0: Fraction, a1: Fraction, a2: Fraction,
                    low: Fraction, up: Fraction) -> Tuple[Fraction, Fraction]:
    """q0 + a1/up < p* < q0 + a2/low."""
    return (q0 + a1 / up, q0 + a2 / low)


def certify(anchor: Fraction, upper_barrier: Fraction, sig_digits: int = 20
            ) -> Tuple[Fraction, Fraction]:
    """Full pipeline: from an anchor below the root and a barrier above it,
    return a certified enclosure (lo, hi) of the threshold.

    Steps:
      1. certificate pair (D, N) for the anchor; require D < N (anchor below);
      2. truncate N/D to sig_digits and apply the Pade value certificates,
         giving A1 < r(anchor)/2 < A2;
      3. bracket H2' on [anchor, barrier] by monotonicity plus bracket_log;
      4. one mean-value step.
    """
    a = anchor.numerator
    b = anchor.denominator
    c = b - a
    d, n = certificate_pair(a, c)
    if d >= n:
        raise ValueError("anchor is not below threshold")

    scale = 10 ** sig_digits
    m_lo = (scale * n) // d
    m_hi = m_lo + 1
    a1 = pade_lower(Fraction(m_lo, scale)) / b / 2
    a2 = pade_upper(Fraction(m_hi, scale)) / b / 2

    low, _ = bracket_log((1 - upper_barrier) / upper_barrier)
    _, up = bracket_log((1 - anchor) / anchor)

    return refinement_step(anchor, a1, a2, low, up)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    p_approx = Fraction("0.110027864438359551261811704334989")
    for budget in [100, 400, 1000]:
        print(f"budget {budget:>5}: best anchor {best_anchor(p_approx, budget)}")
    lo, hi = certify(Fraction(79, 718), Fraction(11002787, 10 ** 8))
    print(f"enclosure lower = {Decimal(lo.numerator) / Decimal(lo.denominator)}")
    print(f"enclosure upper = {Decimal(hi.numerator) / Decimal(hi.denominator)}")
    print(f"width           = {float(hi - lo):.4e}")

visualizations.name: The BB84 Error-Rate Threshold at Three Scales
visualizations.description: A three-panel figure showing the secret-key rate r(Q) = log 2 - 2H2(Q) zooming in on its root by seven orders of magnitude. The left panel shows the whole feasible range with the coarse elementary bracket (6.25%, 12.5%) shaded, making clear how little that bracket says. The middle panel zooms to a window of width 10^-3 and shows the four-decimal certified enclosure together with the anchors 11/100 and 79/718, which are still visually distinguishable. The right panel zooms to a window of width 4 x 10^-8, at which scale the anchor 79/718 sits 9.3 x 10^-9 to the left of the root and the final certified interval, of width 2.17 x 10^-15, is far too small to see.
visualizations.code:
"""Visualization 1 — The secret-key rate and the threshold, at three zoom levels.

Left:   r(Q) = log 2 - 2 H2(Q) across the whole feasible range, with the coarse
        elementary bracket (6.25%, 12.5%) and the root p* marked.
Middle: a zoom onto [0.1095, 0.1105] showing the four-decimal certified
        enclosure and the anchors 11/100 and 79/718.
Right:  a zoom onto a window of width 4e-8 around the root, showing how far the
        continued-fraction anchor 79/718 already sits from 11/100 and how the
        certified thirteen-decimal interval (width 2.17e-15) is invisible at
        this scale.

Produces `bb84_threshold_zoom.png`.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import math
from typing import List, Tuple

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

P_STAR = 0.11002786443835955126


def binary_entropy(p: float) -> float:
    if p <= 0.0 or p >= 1.0:
        return 0.0
    return -p * math.log(p) - (1 - p) * math.log(1 - p)


def key_rate(q: float) -> float:
    return math.log(2) - 2 * binary_entropy(q)


def panel(ax, lo: float, hi: float, title: str, marks: List[Tuple[float, str, str]]) -> None:
    xs = np.linspace(lo, hi, 2000)
    ys = np.array([key_rate(float(x)) for x in xs])
    ax.plot(xs, ys, color="#1f3b73", lw=2.0)
    ax.axhline(0.0, color="#999999", lw=0.9, ls="--")
    for x, label, colour in marks:
        if lo <= x <= hi:
            ax.axvline(x, color=colour, lw=1.2, ls=":")
            ax.annotate(label, xy=(x, 0.0), xytext=(4, 8),
                        textcoords="offset points", fontsize=8, color=colour,
                        rotation=90, va="bottom")
    ax.set_title(title, fontsize=10)
    ax.set_xlabel("quantum bit error rate $Q$")
    ax.grid(alpha=0.25)


def main() -> None:
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(15, 4.4))

    panel(axes[0], 0.001, 0.16,
          "$r(Q)=\\log 2-2H_2(Q)$ and the coarse bracket",
          [(1 / 16, "1/16", "#a03030"), (1 / 8, "1/8", "#a03030"),
           (P_STAR, "$p_\\star$", "#207020")])
    axes[0].axvspan(1 / 16, 1 / 8, color="#a03030", alpha=0.08)
    axes[0].set_ylabel("nats per sifted bit")

    panel(axes[1], 0.1095, 0.1105,
          "four-decimal certified enclosure",
          [(0.11, "11/100", "#c06000"), (79 / 718, "79/718", "#0060c0"),
           (P_STAR, "$p_\\star$", "#207020")])
    axes[1].axvspan(0.1100, 0.1101, color="#207020", alpha=0.10)

    panel(axes[2], P_STAR - 2e-8, P_STAR + 2e-8,
          "anchor $79/718$ vs. the root (window $4\\times10^{-8}$)",
          [(79 / 718, "79/718", "#0060c0"), (P_STAR, "$p_\\star$", "#207020")])
    ticks = [P_STAR - 2e-8, 79 / 718, P_STAR, P_STAR + 2e-8]
    axes[2].set_xticks(ticks)
    axes[2].set_xticklabels([f"{(t - P_STAR) * 1e9:+.1f}" for t in ticks], fontsize=8)
    axes[2].set_xlabel("$Q - p_\\star$   (units of $10^{-9}$)")

    fig.suptitle("The BB84 error-rate threshold at three scales", fontsize=13)
    fig.tight_layout()
    fig.savefig("bb84_threshold_zoom.png", dpi=160)
    print("wrote bb84_threshold_zoom.png")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

visualizations.name: The Quartic Certification Law: Precision versus Certificate Cost
visualizations.description: A log-log plot of certified precision against certificate size (the number of decimal digits of the certificate integers, about 2q log10 q for denominator q). Three families are shown: the distance from each continued-fraction convergent to the threshold; the width approximately 4.9 delta^2 of the enclosure obtained by one mean-value step from that convergent; and, for comparison, the precision that decimal anchors of the same certificate cost achieve under the pure arithmetic scheme. The three lines have slopes corresponding to q^-2, q^-4 and q^-1 respectively, and the vertical gap between the second and third quantifies precisely what Diophantine approximation buys. Two annotations mark the executed certifications: the four-decimal stage, where an 80 000-digit certificate bought 10^-4, and the thirteen-decimal stage, where a 4102-digit certificate bought 2 x 10^-15.
visualizations.code:
"""Visualization 2 — The quartic certification law: cost versus precision.

For each continued-fraction convergent p_k/q_k of the BB84 threshold we plot,
against the certificate size (number of decimal digits of the certificate
integers, ~ 2 q log10 q):

  * the anchor error |p_k/q_k - p*|                          (circles),
  * the width ~ 4.9 * delta^2 of the enclosure produced by one certified
    mean-value step from that anchor                          (squares),
  * for comparison, the precision obtainable by the pure arithmetic scheme at
    the same certificate size, i.e. 1/q                       (triangles).

On log-log axes the three families are straight lines of slopes ~ -2, ~ -4 and
~ -1 in q, and the gap between the squares and the triangles is exactly the
advantage of Diophantine anchoring.  Two annotated points mark the executed
certifications: the four-decimal stage (denominator 10^4, 80000-digit
certificate) and the thirteen-decimal stage (denominator 718, 4102-digit
certificate).

Produces `quartic_law.png`.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import math
from fractions import Fraction
from typing import List, Tuple

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

P_STAR = Fraction("0.1100278644383595512618117043349894601771149050918949")

CONVERGENTS: List[Fraction] = [
    Fraction(1, 9),
    Fraction(11, 100),
    Fraction(34, 309),
    Fraction(79, 718),
    Fraction(16466, 149653),
    Fraction(33011, 300024),
]

DECIMAL_ANCHORS: List[Fraction] = [
    Fraction(1, 10), Fraction(11, 100), Fraction(110, 1000),
    Fraction(1100, 10000), Fraction(11003, 100000),
]


def cert_digits(q: int) -> float:
    """Approximate number of decimal digits of the certificate integers."""
    return 2.0 * q * math.log10(q)


def points(fracs: List[Fraction]) -> Tuple[List[float], List[float], List[float]]:
    sizes, errs, widths = [], [], []
    for f in fracs:
        delta = abs(float(f - P_STAR))
        sizes.append(cert_digits(f.denominator))
        errs.append(delta)
        widths.append(4.9 * delta ** 2)
    return sizes, errs, widths


def main() -> None:
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9.0, 6.0))

    s_c, e_c, w_c = points(CONVERGENTS)
    s_d, e_d, _ = points(DECIMAL_ANCHORS)

    ax.plot(s_c, e_c, "o-", color="#0060c0", label="convergent anchor error $\\delta$")
    ax.plot(s_c, w_c, "s-", color="#207020",
            label="enclosure width after one step $\\approx 4.9\\,\\delta^2$")
    ax.plot(s_d, e_d, "^--", color="#a03030",
            label="decimal anchor error (pure arithmetic scheme)")

    for f, x, y in zip(CONVERGENTS, s_c, w_c):
        ax.annotate(f"{f.numerator}/{f.denominator}", xy=(x, y),
                    xytext=(-10, -16), textcoords="offset points", fontsize=8,
                    color="#207020", ha="right")

    ax.annotate("four-decimal stage:\n80 000-digit certificate\nbuys $10^{-4}$",
                xy=(cert_digits(10000), abs(float(Fraction(1100, 10000) - P_STAR))),
                xytext=(-190, -45), textcoords="offset points", fontsize=9,
                color="#a03030",
                arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color="#a03030"))
    ax.annotate("thirteen-decimal stage:\n4102-digit certificate\nbuys $2\\times10^{-15}$",
                xy=(cert_digits(718), 4.9 * 9.285e-9 ** 2),
                xytext=(55, 45), textcoords="offset points", fontsize=9,
                color="#207020",
                arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color="#207020"))

    ax.set_xscale("log")
    ax.set_yscale("log")
    ax.set_ylim(1e-25, 3e-2)
    ax.set_xlabel("certificate size (decimal digits of the certificate integers)")
    ax.set_ylabel("certified precision")
    ax.set_title("Quartic certification law: precision $\\sim q^{-4}$ at cost $\\sim q^{2}$")
    ax.grid(alpha=0.3, which="both")
    ax.legend(loc="lower left", fontsize=9)

    fig.tight_layout()
    fig.savefig("quartic_law.png", dpi=160)
    print("wrote quartic_law.png")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

interactive_demos.title: The Certification Laboratory: Watch a Transcendental Constant Get Pinned Down
interactive_demos.description: A fully self-contained laboratory in which the reader picks a rational anchor and watches the entire certification pipeline execute in exact arbitrary-precision integer arithmetic, live in the browser. Stage by stage the widget displays: the two certificate integers and their digit count, the exact verdict of the Rational Sign Criterion (below or above threshold) together with the elapsed time, the ratio N/D to twenty-two decimals, the Pade bracket on the key rate at the anchor, the derivative bracket on the interval from the anchor to the certified barrier, and finally the enclosure produced by one mean-value step, with the digits on which the two endpoints agree highlighted -- those are the certified decimals of the threshold. Presets include the continued-fraction convergents 1/9, 11/100, 34/309 and 79/718 along with the generic fraction 76/691; the decisive experiment is to compare 79/718 against 76/691, whose certificates cost the same but which yields six decimals against thirteen. A log-log chart underneath places the reader's chosen anchor among the convergents and the decimal anchors, making the quartic-versus-quadratic tradeoff visible at a glance. Any custom fraction with denominator up to 4000 can be entered.

The Certification Laboratory

The BB84 secret-key rate is r(Q) = log 2 − 2·H₂(Q), and it vanishes at a threshold error rate p⋆ that textbooks quote as “about 11%”. Pick a rational anchor below, and watch the whole certification pipeline run: an exact integer comparison decides which side of the threshold the anchor is on, Padé bounds turn that into a certified value of the key rate, and one mean-value step converts anchor plus derivative bracket into an enclosure of the root. Every integer here is computed exactly (arbitrary-precision arithmetic in your browser).

1 · Choose the anchor

or a custom fraction   / (denominators above ~1500 get slow: the certificate integers have about 2·q·log₁₀q digits)

2 · The Rational Sign Criterion

For p = a/(a+c), the transcendental comparison H₂(p) ⋚ (log 2)/2 is equivalent to the integer comparison D = (a+c)2(a+c) ⋚ N = 2a+c·a2a·c2c. No logarithm is ever evaluated.

3 · Padé value certificate

Since r(a/(a+c)) = log(N/D)/(a+c) exactly, the cubic-accuracy bounds 2(x−1)/(x+1) ≤ log x ≤ (x−1/x)/2 convert the integer bracket on N/D into a certified bracket on the key rate.

4 · Derivative bracket

H₂′(x) = log((1−x)/x) is strictly decreasing, so on [anchor, barrier] it is bracketed by its two endpoint values. The barrier 0.11002787 is the certified upper bound from the previous stage.

In the certified argument these two numbers come from the Padé bounds applied to log(639/79) and log(88997213/11002787) after splitting off a factor 8 = 2³. Here they are recomputed in double precision and then widened by 10⁻⁹ so the displayed bracket is safely valid.

5 · One mean-value step

If A₁ < r(q₀)/2 < A₂ and L ≤ H₂′ ≤ U on [q₀, q₁] with q₀ < p⋆ < q₁, then q₀ + A₁/U < p⋆ < q₀ + A₂/L.

Highlighted digits are the ones the two endpoints agree on: those decimals of p⋆ are certified. The true value begins 0.1100278644383595512618… Compare 79/718 with 76/691: the two certificates cost essentially the same, but the continued-fraction convergent yields thirteen decimals where the generic fraction of the same size yields six. One caveat worth seeing for yourself: the Padé bounds are sharp only when N/D is close to 1, i.e. when (a+c)·r is small, so a large denominator at a rate far from the threshold is doubly penalised.

7 · Why continued fractions win

Certificate cost grows like q², but a convergent of denominator q sits only ≈ q⁻² from the root, and the mean-value step squares that — so precision improves like q⁻⁴. Precision beats cost by exactly a factor of two in the exponent.

# Pinning Down Eleven Percent *A guided tour of how a transcendental constant of quantum cryptography gets nailed to thirteen decimal places — using nothing but whole numbers, one inequality about logarithms, and a two-hundred-year-old idea from number theory.* --- ## 1. The number everybody quotes In the BB84 quantum key distribution protocol, Alice sends photons in randomly chosen polarization bases and Bob measures in randomly chosen bases. Where the bases agree, they should get the same bit; the fraction of places where they disagree is the **quantum bit error rate** $Q$. Noise causes disagreements — and so does an eavesdropper, indistinguishably. The standard security analysis gives an asymptotic secret-key rate, in nats per sifted bit, of $$r(Q) \;=\; \log 2 \;-\; 2\,H_2(Q), \qquad H_2(p) \;=\; -p\log p - (1-p)\log(1-p).$$ One factor of $H_2(Q)$ pays for error reconciliation; the other pays for privacy amplification. When they consume the whole bit $\log 2$, nothing is left. The error rate at which that happens is the threshold $p_\star$, universally quoted as "about $11\%$". It is worth pausing on how little that statement actually says. $p_\star$ solves a transcendental equation with no closed form; the figure $0.11$ is a floating-point computation someone did once and everyone repeated. The best *rigorous* bracket you get from elementary arguments is $$6.25\% \;<\; p_\star \;<\; 12.5\%,$$ which cannot even distinguish $11\%$ from $12\%$. {{visualization:0}}
Why is the rate $\log 2 - 2H_2(Q)$? (click to expand) Think of one sifted bit as one unit of raw shared randomness, worth $\log 2$ nats. Two taxes are levied on it. Alice must send Bob enough classical information to correct his errors; by Shannon's source coding theorem with side information, this costs $H_2(Q)$ per bit. And Alice and Bob must destroy whatever correlation the eavesdropper holds; for a collective attack on BB84, the eavesdropper's information is also bounded by $H_2(Q)$ per bit, so privacy amplification costs that much again. What survives is $\log 2 - 2H_2(Q)$. Dividing by $\log 2$ gives the familiar base-two form $1 - 2h(Q)$. The reader who prefers a reference point: everything below is about the [binary entropy function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binary_entropy_function) and its level set at half a bit.
--- ## 2. Turning a transcendental into an integer Here is the first move, and it is the one that makes everything else possible. Write a rational error rate as $p = a/(a+c)$ with $a$ and $c$ positive integers. Substitute into $H_2$ and clear the denominator: $$2(a+c)\,H_2\!\left(\frac{a}{a+c}\right) = 2(a+c)\log(a+c) - 2a\log a - 2c\log c.$$ Every logarithm now carries an *integer* coefficient. Compare against $2(a+c)\cdot\frac{\log 2}{2} = (a+c)\log 2$ and exponentiate: the logarithms vanish, and we are left with > **The Rational Sign Criterion.** > $$H_2\!\left(\frac{a}{a+c}\right) < \frac{\log 2}{2} > \iff > (a+c)^{2(a+c)} \;<\; 2^{\,a+c}\,a^{2a}\,c^{2c}.$$ This is an *equivalence*, so it is a complete decision procedure. Feed it any rational error rate and one comparison of two whole numbers settles, with certainty, whether the protocol survives there. {{algorithm:0}} At $11/100$ the comparison is $100^{200}$ against $2^{100}\cdot 11^{22}\cdot 89^{178}$: two 823-digit integers, and the left one is smaller, so $11\%$ is safely below threshold. At $1101/10000$ it takes 80 000-digit integers, and the comparison goes the other way. Together: $0.1100 < p_\star < 0.1101$.
Why this stops working (the brute-force wall) The certificate at denominator $b$ involves integers with about $2b\log_{10}b$ digits. Each new decimal multiplies $b$ by ten, hence the digit count by ten and the arithmetic by a hundred. At $b = 10^7$ you would need several numbers of $10^8$ digits each. The mathematics is still perfectly correct — the criterion never stops being an equivalence — but the cost curve wins. Four or five decimals is where brute force dies.
--- ## 3. From *which side* to *how far* To get past the wall we need to stop asking for signs and start asking for values. Fortunately the same algebra gives an exact formula: the key rate at a rational point is a scaled logarithm of a rational number, $$r\!\left(\frac{a}{a+c}\right) = \frac{1}{a+c}\,\log\frac{N}{D}, \qquad N = 2^{\,a+c}a^{2a}c^{2c},\quad D = (a+c)^{2(a+c)}.$$ So certified numbers for $r$ reduce to certified numbers for $\log$ near $1$. The right tool is the **Padé bound of order $(1,1)$**: $$\frac{2(x-1)}{x+1} \;\le\; \log x \;\le\; \frac{x - x^{-1}}{2}, \qquad x \ge 1.$$
The one-line proof Both differences vanish at $x = 1$, and $$\frac{d}{dx}\left[\log x - \frac{2(x-1)}{x+1}\right] = \frac{(x-1)^2}{x(x+1)^2} \ge 0, \qquad \frac{d}{dx}\left[\frac{x-x^{-1}}{2} - \log x\right] = \frac{(x-1)^2}{2x^2} \ge 0.$$ A non-negative derivative starting from zero stays non-negative. That is the entire argument — no series, no remainder terms. The error of both bounds is cubic in $x-1$, against quadratic for the naive $1 - 1/x \le \log x \le x-1$. At $x = 1.0000279$ that difference is the difference between eight decimals and thirteen.
{{algorithm:1}} --- ## 4. One honest step of Newton Knowing the value of $r$ at a nearby point, and knowing how steeply it falls, locates the root. Newton's method does this approximately; the mean value theorem does it *with proof*. > **The Refinement Step.** Suppose $q_0 < p_\star < q_1$, and that we have > certified $A_1 < \tfrac12 r(q_0) < A_2$ and $L \le H_2'(x) \le U$ for all > $x \in [q_0,q_1]$, with $L > 0$. Then > $$q_0 + \frac{A_1}{U} \;<\; p_\star \;<\; q_0 + \frac{A_2}{L}.$$ The proof is three lines: the mean value theorem gives a $\xi$ between $q_0$ and $p_\star$ with $H_2'(\xi)(p_\star - q_0) = H_2(p_\star) - H_2(q_0) = \tfrac12 r(q_0)$; then bound $H_2'(\xi)$ above and below and divide. The consequence is the **quadratic law**: because the derivative bracket must cover the gap between anchor and root, its width $U - L$ is itself proportional to that gap. An anchor at distance $\delta$ therefore yields an enclosure of width roughly $4.9\,\delta^2$. And *that* changes the whole problem. It is no longer "how much arithmetic can I afford?" but "how good an anchor can I find?". --- ## 5. Decimals are the wrong numbers Anchoring at $11/100$ gives $\delta = 2.79\times10^{-5}$ and hence eight decimals. To do better with decimals you would need a $10^7$ denominator — the hundred-megabyte integers we already ruled out. But nothing requires the anchor to be a decimal. And rational numbers are wildly unequal in accuracy-per-denominator. The tool for exploiting this is the [continued fraction expansion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continued_fraction), whose truncations — the **convergents** — are provably the best rational approximations of a real number: no fraction with a smaller denominator comes closer. For the BB84 threshold, $$p_\star = [\,0;\,9,\,11,\,3,\,2,\,208,\,2,\,12,\ldots\,],$$ with convergents $$\frac01,\ \frac19,\ \frac{11}{100},\ \frac{34}{309},\ \frac{79}{718},\ \frac{16466}{149653},\ \frac{33011}{300024},\ \ldots$$ Look at the third one. **The textbook value $11/100$ is a convergent.** By the best-approximation theorem, $11\%$ is the closest any fraction with denominator below $309$ ever gets to the threshold. The folk value is not a lazy rounding; it is optimal for its size. Now look at the fifth. $79/718$ has a three-digit denominator — its certificate uses 4102-digit integers, *twenty times smaller* than the 80 000-digit four-decimal certificate — and it sits only $9.29\times10^{-9}$ from the root, three thousand times closer than $11/100$. {{visualization:1}} {{algorithm:2}} --- ## 6. Run the pipeline yourself Everything above comes together in the laboratory below. Pick an anchor, and it computes the exact certificate integers in your browser, decides the sign, builds the Padé value bracket, brackets the derivative, and takes the mean-value step — showing you exactly how many decimals of $p_\star$ come out the other end. The instructive experiment: compare $79/718$ with $76/691$. Their certificates cost essentially the same. The convergent gives thirteen decimals; the generic fraction gives six. {{interactive_demo:0}}
What the three certified ingredients look like for $79/718$ **Position and value.** $718^{1436} < 2^{718}\cdot 79^{158}\cdot 639^{1278}$, so the anchor is below threshold. Sharpening, $$100002787345813950188 \cdot 718^{1436} < 10^{20}\cdot 2^{718}79^{158}639^{1278} < 100002787345813950189\cdot 718^{1436},$$ which through the Padé bounds gives $3.882043130930\times10^{-8} < r(79/718) < 3.882043131686\times10^{-8}$. **Derivative.** $H_2'(x) = \log\frac{1-x}{x}$ is decreasing, so on $[79/718,\,0.11002787]$ it lies between $\log\frac{88997213}{11002787}$ and $\log\frac{639}{79}$. Both are close to $8$; splitting off $8 = 2^3$ and applying the Padé bounds to the residue gives $$2.0904563381 \le H_2'(x) \le 2.0904568254.$$ **The step.** Feeding these into the refinement step gives an interval of width $2.17\times10^{-15}$: $$0.1100278644383 < p_\star < 0.1100278644384.$$
--- ## 7. The result > **Thirteen Certified Decimals.** The unique quantum bit error rate at which the > asymptotic one-way BB84 secret-key rate vanishes satisfies > $$0.1100278644383 < p_\star < 0.1100278644384, > \qquad \lfloor 10^{13} p_\star \rfloor = 1100278644383.$$ Two consequences worth recording. The classical figure is *safe but conservative*: $p_\star > 11/100$, with the certified gap $$2.786\times10^{-5} < |p_\star - 0.11| < 2.787\times10^{-5},$$ so quoting $11\%$ understates the tolerable error rate. And the rate at exactly $11\%$ is $1.16506723\ldots\times10^{-4}$ nats per sifted bit — about one secret bit per six thousand sifted bits. {{demo:0}} --- ## 8. The economics: a quartic law Step back and the whole thing is a race between two exponents. | resource | scaling in the denominator $q$ | |---|---| | certificate cost | $\sim q^{2}$ | | convergent's distance to the root $\delta$ | $\sim q^{-2}$ | | enclosure width after one step $\approx 4.9\delta^2$ | $\sim q^{-4}$ | Precision improves twice as fast as cost grows. To reach width $\varepsilon$ costs about $\varepsilon^{-1/2}$ arithmetic, rather than the $\varepsilon^{-1}$ that digit-by-digit certification demands. That is the entire reason a 718-denominator anchor demolishes a $10^4$-denominator one. Extrapolating: the next convergent $16466/149653$ would reach about $10^{-21}$, and somewhere near eighteen decimals a *different* ingredient — the certified accuracy of $\log 2$ itself — becomes the binding constraint.
Does thirteen decimals of a security threshold matter? No experimentalist will measure a quantum bit error rate to $10^{-13}$. But that is not really the point, for two reasons. *As a reference value*: security parameters get composed, propagated, and compared through finite-key analyses and decoy-state estimates. A threshold known only as "about $11\%$" injects an unquantified $2.8\times10^{-5}$ into every downstream statement. Now it is quantified exactly. *As a method*: the pipeline — exact integer criterion, rational-function bounds proved from monotonicity, continued-fraction anchor, one mean-value step — is not specific to the binary entropy. Capacity thresholds, cutoff rates, percolation constants, fixed points of entropy inequalities: all are currently known the way $11\%$ was known.
--- ## 9. Where to go next The conjecture the whole development points at: *for any real-analytic $f$ with a simple root whose sign at rationals is decidable by an integer comparison of size $O(b\log b)$, a certified enclosure of width $\varepsilon$ costs $O(\varepsilon^{-1/2})$, achieved by anchoring at convergents.* A second-order Taylor step would push the exponent to $1/3$. The threshold at which quantum cryptography stops working is $0.1100278644383\ldots$ — and the fastest route to those digits ran, of all places, through the theory of continued fractions.
